summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) and systemic thyroid emergencies. This poster covers interpreting TFTs, managing life-threatening storms, and navigating the surgical rehabilitation of the Graves' orbit.

sections.title: Defining Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
sections.content: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves’ Orbitopathy, is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Interpreting Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)
content: Scenario: A 45-year-old female presents with eyelid retraction. Labs: Suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4.
Definition: Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis) – excessive secretion of thyroid hormones.
Examiner's Pick: Suppressed TSH with high T4/T3 is classic for Graves' disease.
High Yield: Severity of TED often does not parallel serum levels of T3 or T4.
Red Flag: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) are specific markers for Graves' and correlate with eye disease activity.

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Medical Emergency – Thyrotoxic Storm
content: Clinical Picture: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), dehydration, tachycardia (>140 bpm), heart failure, and coma.
Scenario: Patient with known Graves’ presenting for surgery with Temp 41°C, HR 150 bpm, and extreme agitation.
TREATMENT DOSES:
Beta-blockers: Propranolol (40 mg PO or 1 mg slow IV) to control heart rate.
Antithyroid Drugs: Carbimazole (15–25 mg Q6H PO) or Propylthiouracil.
Iodine: Lugol’s solution (0.3 mL PO Q8H) to block hormone release.
Corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q6H IV) to block T4-to-T3 conversion.

sections.title: Scenario 3: The Hypothyroid Emergency – Myxoedema Coma
content: Clinical Picture: Hypothermia (34°C), bradycardia (45 bpm), hypotension, seizures, and 'myxoedema madness'.
Management Step 1: Thyroid replacement with T3 (5–20 µg IV Q12H) or Levothyroxine.
Management Step 2: Steroids – Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q8H IV) if pituitary involvement is suspected.
Pitfall: Avoid rapid rewarming; treat infections and hypoglycemia concurrently.

sections.title: Scenario 4: Sight-Threatening TED (CON)
content: Diagnosis: Compressive Optic Neuropathy (CON).
Clinical Scenario: 'Washed out' colors, reduced vision, and positive RAPD.
Mechanism: Crowding of the orbital apex by enlarged EOMs.
Treatment: Pulse Steroids – IV Methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for 3 days).
Emergency Surgery: Urgent orbital decompression if steroids fail within 48–72 hours.

rows: Tachycardia, Tremor, Heat intolerance, Weight loss, Goiter
Bradycardia, Cold intolerance, Weight gain, Dry skin, Constipation

sections.title: Scenario 5: Exposure Keratopathy in TED
content: Clinical Picture: Incomplete blink (lagophthalmos), inferior punctate erosions, and possible bacterial keratitis.
Scenario: 26 mm proptosis with central corneal infiltrate.
Management: Intensive lubricants, nocturnal eyelid taping, or Moisture goggles.
Hazard: Permanent vision loss from corneal perforation.

sections.title: Smoking Key Points
sections.content: Smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED progression. Smokers are 7–10 times more likely to develop TED and have a longer active phase (2–3 years vs. 1 year in non-smokers).

sections.title: Scenario 9 & 10: Signs & Management
content: Restrictive Myopathy: Persistent 20-prism diopter hypotropia in TED.
Strabismus Management: Recession only (avoid resection due to fibrosis). Delay until 6 months of stability.
Eyelid Signs: Dalrymple sign (retraction at rest), von Graefe sign (lid lag on downgaze).

branches: Diagnosis (2 of 3): Immune dysfunction, Ocular signs (Proptosis/CON), Imaging (Tendon-sparing EOM)
Assessment: CAS Score (Pain, redness, swelling). Score ≥ 3/7 = Active
Tiered Rx: Mild (Lubes, Selenium 100µg BD), Mod/Severe (Steroids), Sight-Threat (CON)

sections.title: Clinical Phases: Active vs. Quiescent (Rundle’s Curve)
content: Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months. Requires immunosuppression.
Quiescent Phase: 'Burned-out' phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease.

sections.title: Systemic Hazards & Precautions
content: Radioactive Iodine (RAI): Can exacerbate/trigger TED. Precaution: Co-administer oral steroids (Prednisone).
Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Occurs in 5% of TED. Suspect MG if PTOSIS is present instead of lid retraction.
Timolol Glaucoma Meds: Can mask hyperthyroid tachycardia. Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate thyroid storm.
Surgical Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until euthyroid and stable for 6–9 months.

Best for identifying active muscle inflammation via increased water content.
Tendons are characteristically SPARED in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).

sections.title: Management Pearls & New Horizons
content: Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% acts as 'chemical sympathectomy' for temporary relief of lid retraction.
Highlight: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) is a new FDA-approved biologic that effectively reduces proptosis in active disease.
Pediatric Fact: TED is rare in children; symptoms are milder and vision loss is exceptional.
Order of Rehab: Decompression changes orbital volume and must be done first as it alters muscle/lid position.

data.generationPrompt:
Thyroid Disorders in Ophthalmic Practice: Internal Medicine & Emergencies
Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves’ Orbitopathy, is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OSCE & VIVA Clinical Scenarios
Scenario 1: Interpreting Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs)
Scenario: A 45-year-old female presents with eyelid retraction. Her labs show a suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4.
Definition: Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis) – excessive secretion of thyroid hormones.
Examiner's Pick: Suppressed TSH with high T4/T3 is classic for Graves' disease.
High Yield: Severity of TED often does not parallel serum levels of T3 or T4.
Red Flag: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) are specific markers for Graves' and correlate with eye disease activity.
Scenario 2: The Medical Emergency – Thyrotoxic Storm
Scenario: A patient with known Graves’ disease presents for surgery but is found to have a temperature of 41°C, tachycardia of 150 bpm, and extreme agitation.
Clinical Picture: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), dehydration, tachycardia (>140 bpm), heart failure, and coma.
Treatment (Drug Doses):
Beta-blockers: Propranolol (40 mg PO or 1 mg slow IV) to control heart rate.
Antithyroid Drugs: Carbimazole (15–25 mg Q6H PO) or Propylthiouracil.
Iodine: Lugol’s solution (0.3 mL PO Q8H) to block hormone release.
Corticosteroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q6H IV) to block T4-to-T3 conversion.
Scenario 3: The Hypothyroid Emergency – Myxoedema Coma
Scenario: An elderly patient is found unresponsive in the ward with a heart rate of 45 bpm and a core temperature of 34°C.
Clinical Picture: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, seizures, and "myxoedema madness".
Management:
Thyroid replacement: T3 (5–20 µg IV Q12H) or Levothyroxine.
Steroids: Hydrocortisone (100 mg Q8H IV) if pituitary involvement is suspected.
Pitfall: Avoid rapid rewarming; treat infections and hypoglycemia concurrently.
Scenario 4: Sight-Threatening TED (Compressive Optic Neuropathy)
Scenario: A patient with severe TED reports "washed out" colors and reduced vision. You note a positive RAPD.
Diagnosis: Compressive Optic Neuropathy (CON).
Mechanism: Crowding of the orbital apex by enlarged EOMs.
Treatment:
Pulse Steroids: IV Methylprednisolone (500 mg–1 g daily for 3 days).
Emergency Surgery: Urgent orbital decompression if steroids fail within 48–72 hours.
Scenario 5: Exposure Keratopathy in TED
Scenario: A patient with 26 mm proptosis and severe eyelid retraction presents with a central corneal infiltrate.
Clinical Picture: Incomplete blink (lagophthalmos), inferior punctate erosions, and possible bacterial keratitis.
Management: Intensive lubricants, nocturnal eyelid taping, or Moisture goggles.
Hazard: Permanent vision loss from corneal perforation.
Scenario 6: The Smoking Risk Factor
Scenario: The examiner asks, "What is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED progression?"
Answer: Smoking.
Key Point: Smokers are 7–10 times more likely to develop TED and have a longer active phase (2–3 years vs. 1 year in non-smokers).
Scenario 7: Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Hazard
Scenario: A patient with mild TED is scheduled for RAI for hyperthyroidism.
Hazard: RAI can exacerbate or trigger TED.
Precaution: Co-administer oral steroids (Prednisone) during treatment to prevent progression.
Scenario 8: Pediatric TED
Scenario: A 10-year-old presents with bilateral proptosis and hyperthyroidism.
Key Point: TED is rare in children; symptoms are usually milder, and vision loss is exceptional.
DDx: Rule out orbital cellulitis, rhabdomyosarcoma, or neuroblastoma.
Scenario 9: Restrictive Myopathy and Diplopia
Scenario: A patient with stable TED has a persistent 20-prism diopter hypotropia in the right eye.
Muscle Involvement Order (IMSLO): Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.
Management: Strabismus surgery (recession only, avoid resection due to fibrosis).
Precaution: Surgery must be delayed until measurements are stable for at least 6 months.
Scenario 10: Eyelid Retraction Differential Diagnosis
Scenario: A patient has a "staring look" but normal thyroid tests.
Ocular Signs: Dalrymple sign (retraction at rest), von Graefe sign (lid lag on downgaze).
DDx: Parinaud syndrome (Collier sign), 3rd nerve misdirection, Myasthenia Gravis (Hering’s law), or orbital mass.
Scenario 11: Active vs. Quiescent TED (Rundle’s Curve)
Scenario: Describe the clinical course of TED.
Active Phase: Congestive stage, red/painful eyes, lasts 6–18 months.
Quiescent Phase: "Burned-out" phase, white eyes but persistent fibrosis/motility defects.
Examiner's Pick: Clinical Activity Score (CAS) ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease requiring immunosuppression.
Scenario 12: Systemic Associations (Autoimmune)
Scenario: What other diseases should you screen for in a TED patient?
Answer: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) (occurs in up to 5% of TED patients).
Clinical Pearl: Suspect MG if the patient has ptosis instead of lid retraction.
Scenario 13: Order of Surgical Rehabilitation
Scenario: A patient needs several surgeries for TED. What is the correct sequence?
Sequence: 1. Orbital Decompression → 2. Strabismus Surgery → 3. Eyelid Surgery.
Rationale: Decompression changes orbital volume and can alter muscle alignment and lid position.
Scenario 14: Orbital Imaging in TED (CT vs. MRI)
Scenario: Which imaging modality is preferred for TED and why?
CT: Best for bony resolution and planning decompression.
MRI (T2/STIR): Best for identifying active muscle inflammation (water content).
Key Point: Tendons are characteristically spared in TED (unlike orbital pseudotumor).
Scenario 15: Complications of Glaucoma Meds in Thyroid Disease
Scenario: You prescribe Timolol for a patient with TED and hyperthyroidism.
Hazard: Topical beta-blockers can mask symptoms of hyperthyroidism (e.g., tachycardia).
Precaution: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers can precipitate a thyroid storm.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map (The "TED Algorithm")
Diagnosis (2 of 3 signs):
Immune thyroid dysfunction (Graves/Hashimoto).
Ocular signs (Lid retraction, proptosis, CON).
Imaging findings (Tendon-sparing EOM enlargement).
Assessment of Activity:
CAS Score: Pain, redness, swelling (Score ≥ 3/7 = Active).
Tiered Management:
Mild: Lubricants, smoking cessation, Selenium (100 µg BD).
Moderate/Severe: Oral Prednisone or pulsed IV Methylprednisolone.
Sight-Threatening (CON): Urgent IV Steroids → Orbital Decompression.
Rehabilitation Sequence:
Decompress → Squint → Lids.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: Apraclonidine 0.5% can be used as a "chemical sympathectomy" for temporary relief of lid retraction while waiting for stabilization.
Pitfall: Do not perform strabismus or lid surgery until the patient has been euthyroid and measurements stable for 6–9 months.
Examiner's Pick: In CON, the orbital apex is the site of maximal compression; CT scans will show "apical crowding".
Highlight: Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) is a new FDA-approved biologic that effectively reduces proptosis in active disease.
High Yield: Platelet count and ESR are important to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) in elderly patients presenting with AION-like vision loss.
